title: Dred Scott’s Descendant and Taney’s Heir Confront a Legacy That Still Divides the Court
summary:
In a Capitol Hill church last week, two people bound by one of America’s most infamous Supreme Court cases came together. Lynne Jackson is the great-great-granddaughter of Dred Scott, the enslaved man who sued for his freedom in 1857. Charlie Taney is the great-great-grandnephew of Chief Justice Roger Taney, who wrote the opinion declaring that Black people “had no rights which the white man was bound to respect.” Their meeting came just days after the current Supreme Court issued a landmark ruling on birthright citizenship — a direct descendant of the legal battle Scott started.

The 1857 Dred Scott decision held that enslaved people were not U.S. citizens and could not sue in federal court. It is widely considered the worst ruling in the court’s history and a catalyst for the Civil War. The 14th Amendment, adopted after the war, overturned it by guaranteeing citizenship to “all persons born or naturalized in the United States.” Last week, in a 5-4 decision, the Supreme Court affirmed that almost all babies born on U.S. soil are citizens, rejecting the Trump administration’s attempt to limit birthright citizenship.

Chief Justice John Roberts, writing for the majority, declared that “citizenship, then and now, was the right to have rights.” But Justice Clarence Thomas dissented, arguing the 14th Amendment was intended only for freed slaves and their children. “I am not sure that today’s opinion will stand the test of time,” he wrote. The narrow margin — one vote — underscored how fragile these protections can be.

Jackson, who runs the Dred Scott Heritage Foundation, called her ancestor’s case “a major catalyst for the Civil War.” Taney acknowledged his family’s painful legacy, quoting the opinion’s racist language with visible discomfort. Their joint appearance was a powerful reminder that the questions Dred Scott raised — about race, citizenship, and belonging — are still being fought over in the highest court in the land.
why_it_matters: The legacy of slavery continues to echo in America's highest court, directly affecting who is considered a citizen — a right that determines access to education, jobs, and even voting — and one that could be challenged again, shaping the democracy you inherit.

background_read: The Dred Scott case is widely considered the worst Supreme Court decision in American history. In 1857, the Court ruled 7-2 that Dred Scott, an enslaved man who had lived in a free state, could not sue for his freedom because Black people were not and could never be citizens. The ruling deepened the divide over slavery and is seen as a catalyst for the Civil War (1861–1865).

After the Union won the Civil War, the 14th Amendment was added to the Constitution in 1868 and directly overturned the Dred Scott decision. It guarantees that 'all persons born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof, are citizens.' This is the foundation of birthright citizenship.

In recent years, some politicians and legal scholars have argued that the 14th Amendment should not apply to children of undocumented immigrants or temporary residents. The Trump administration tried to limit birthright citizenship through an executive order in 2025, leading to the Supreme Court case described in the article.

Chief Justice John Roberts is the current Chief Justice of the United States, appointed by a Republican president. Justice Clarence Thomas, the longest-serving current justice, is known for his conservative and originalist views. He frequently argues that the original meaning of the Constitution should guide all decisions.

Lynne Jackson runs the Dred Scott Heritage Foundation to educate people about her ancestor's legacy. Charlie Taney carries the burden of his ancestor Roger Taney's name, and their joint public appearances are a deliberate act of reconciliation and a reminder that the wounds of slavery still echo in today's legal battles.

perspectives.description: The Supreme Court's affirmation of broad birthright citizenship protects a foundational right for millions of Americans, including children of immigrants. It reinforces the 14th Amendment's promise and ensures that nearly all born on U.S. soil have full legal status and opportunity from birth.

The narrow 5-4 decision and Justice Thomas's dissent reveal how fragile this right is. A future Supreme Court with different appointees could reverse it, plunging millions into legal limbo and renewing deep racial wounds that many thought had healed. The opinion's language echoes past injustices.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral – Historical pattern of the Court
perspectives.description: The Dred Scott case and the recent birthright ruling both show how the Supreme Court's interpretation of citizenship can swing dramatically with the political and social tides. Constitutional amendments can overturn decisions, but until then, the Court holds immense power to define who belongs—a pattern that has played out repeatedly over 160 years.

Future legal challenges may test birthright citizenship again, perhaps through new executive orders or legislation aiming to exclude certain groups. The public's understanding of the 14th Amendment and its guarantees will be crucial in defending it. The meeting of two descendants serves as a reminder that this debate is far from over and could define American identity for the next generation.
